spec: spec/saas-api.md § GET /v1/cache/{key} (response headers) and § Remaining Freshness
ci_verification: tools/freshness-headers-verify.py (stdlib only; with a mutation self-test)
contract: Each row is one header's value on a `GET` `200 OK`: `value` is the field value, or null when the response does not carry the header. A field value is bytes, so each character of `value` stands for one byte (U+0000 to U+00FF, as the Fetch Standard models header values). No `value` starts or ends with a space or tab: RFC 9110 §5.5 excludes that white space from the field value, and HTTP stacks differ in whether they strip it before a parser sees it. No `value` holds a control character other than tab: RFC 9110's field-value grammar excludes them, and stacks differ in what they do with one. In `freshness_vectors` the header is `X-CacheKit-Freshness` and `stale` is how the SDK must classify the response: fresh when the header is absent or exactly `fresh`, stale for any other value. In `fresh_for_vectors` the header is `X-CacheKit-Fresh-For` and `fresh_for` is the bound the SDK must read, in seconds: the value's number when it is 1 to 7 ASCII digits and at most 2,592,000, otherwise 0, and null when the header is absent (no server-side bound). An SDK conforms when its parser, handed each `value` as its HTTP stack would deliver those bytes, returns `stale` or `fresh_for`.

freshness_vectors.name: freshness_absent
freshness_vectors.note: No header: pre-SWR servers do not emit it, so the response is fresh; a parser that treats a missing header as an unrecognized value reads it as stale.

freshness_vectors.name: freshness_stale
freshness_vectors.note: The `stale` token: a stale hit, never an error; a parser that knows only `fresh` raises on it.

freshness_vectors.name: freshness_capitalised
freshness_vectors.note: Tokens are case-sensitive, so `Fresh` is unrecognized and stale; a parser that compares case-insensitively reads it as fresh.

freshness_vectors.name: freshness_uppercase_stale
freshness_vectors.note: Unrecognized, so stale; a parser that looks only for the exact token `stale` reads it as fresh.

freshness_vectors.name: freshness_empty
freshness_vectors.note: An empty value is present, not absent, so it is unrecognized and stale; a parser that tests the value's truthiness reads it as fresh.

freshness_vectors.name: freshness_nbsp_suffix
freshness_vectors.note: `fresh` and a no-break space (byte 0xA0), which HTTP keeps: unrecognized, so stale. Python's `str.strip()` and JavaScript's `trim()` drop it and read fresh.

freshness_vectors.name: freshness_list_fresh_first
freshness_vectors.note: A list, as a recipient that combines repeated field lines delivers it (RFC 9110 §5.3), is not the token `fresh`; a parser that reads the first item, checks a prefix or looks for `fresh` anywhere reads it as fresh.

freshness_vectors.name: freshness_list_fresh_last
freshness_vectors.note: The same list in the other order; a parser that reads the last item reads it as fresh.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_absent
fresh_for_vectors.note: No header: a no-expiry entry, or a pre-signal server. No server-side bound applies, so the SDK's configured local TTL does; a parser that reads it as 0 never backfills from a pre-signal server.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_zero
fresh_for_vectors.note: Zero is valid: freshness is spent, so the response is not backfilled; a parser that turns 0 into no value (`or None`, `|| undefined`) applies no bound.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_one
fresh_for_vectors.note: The smallest positive bound.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_seven_digits
fresh_for_vectors.note: Seven digits with leading zeros is valid; a parser that rejects leading zeros reads 0.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_cap
fresh_for_vectors.note: The 30-day cap itself is valid; a parser whose range check excludes it reads 0.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_empty
fresh_for_vectors.note: Empty is present but not 1 to 7 digits, so 0; a parser that treats it as absent applies no bound.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_negative
fresh_for_vectors.note: Signed, so 0; a parser that accepts a sign reads -1.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_plus_sign
fresh_for_vectors.note: Signed, so 0; Python's `int()` and JavaScript's `Number()` and `parseInt` read 5.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_decimal
fresh_for_vectors.note: A decimal point, so 0; `Number()` and `parseInt` read 5.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_exponent
fresh_for_vectors.note: An exponent, so 0; `Number()` reads 1000 and `parseInt` 1.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_hex
fresh_for_vectors.note: A hex prefix, so 0; `Number()`, and `parseInt` without a radix, read 16.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_digit_separator
fresh_for_vectors.note: An underscore, so 0; Python's `int()` reads 10 and `parseInt` 1.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_inner_space
fresh_for_vectors.note: White space inside the value, so 0; `parseInt` reads 1, and a parser that drops white space reads 10.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_nbsp_prefix
fresh_for_vectors.note: A no-break space (byte 0xA0), then 5: not 1 to 7 ASCII digits, so 0. HTTP keeps the byte, and Python's `str.strip()` and JavaScript's `trim()` drop it and read 5.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_eight_digits
fresh_for_vectors.note: Eight digits, so 0 although the number is 5: the grammar bounds the length as well as the value.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_over_cap
fresh_for_vectors.note: One over the cap, so 0; a parser without the range check reads 2,592,001.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_wraps_32_bit
fresh_for_vectors.note: 2^32 + 2,592,000, ten digits, so 0: a parser that skips the length check and converts to a wrapping 32-bit integer reads 2,592,000, which its range check then passes.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_over_64_bits
fresh_for_vectors.note: 2^64 + 2,592,000, twenty digits, so 0: a parser that skips the length check reads 2,592,000 through a wrapping 64-bit integer, and one that converts first and reads the overflow as no value applies no bound.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_4301_digits
fresh_for_vectors.note: 4,301 digits, so 0: Python's `int()` refuses a string of more than 4,300 digits, so a parser that converts before it checks the length raises.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_superscript_two
fresh_for_vectors.note: The byte 0xB2, `²` in Latin-1: not an ASCII digit, so 0. Python's `str.isdigit()` accepts it, and `int()` then raises.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_arabic_indic_one
fresh_for_vectors.note: The UTF-8 bytes of U+0661 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT ONE: not ASCII digits, so 0. Decoded as UTF-8, Python's `str.isdigit()` and `int()` accept it as 1.

fresh_for_vectors.name: fresh_for_list
fresh_for_vectors.note: A list, as a recipient that combines repeated field lines delivers it: not 1 to 7 digits, so 0; `parseInt` reads 5.
